body: Ikenberry, Lakonishok and Vermaelen, 'Market Underreaction to Open Market Share Repurchases' (Journal of Financial Economics 39(2-3), 1995; ~1,900 citations), 1,239 US repurchase announcements 1980-1990: the average announcement return was about +3.5%, followed by an average four-year buy-and-hold abnormal return of about +12.1%. For high book-to-market (value) repurchasers the four-year abnormal return was about +45.3%; for glamour stocks it was roughly nil. The market underreacts to the undervaluation signal. Peyer and Vermaelen, 'The Nature and Persistence of Buyback Anomalies' (Review of Financial Studies 22(4), 2009; ~380 citations): the anomaly still existed through 2004, was strongest after large price declines and analyst downgrades, and is consistent with overreaction to bad news. Fu, Huang and Lin (SSRN 2011; later Management Science) report that long-run buyback and SEO anomalies weakened markedly after the early 2000s; single-source, so treat as unverified. Replicated: announcement effects are robust worldwide; long-run drift is sample-dependent. Use for us: in India, buybacks have mostly been tender offers by cash-rich IT, PSU and MNC firms, and taxation changed three times in 2024-26 (insight:india-dividend-buyback-tax), so US results transfer loosely. The informative case is a promoter-backed buyback (or promoter not tendering) in a beaten-down, cheap, cash-generative firm. Routine buybacks by richly valued large caps carry little signal. Buffett's rule (price-dependent repurchase) is the right filter.
title: Open-market buybacks: +3.5% on announcement and +12% over 4 years, +45% for value stocks (Ikenberry-Lakonishok-Vermaelen 1995); persistence debated after 2000s
